newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chirac challenges U.S. in Japan agreement.
newsitem.headline: Chirac challenges U.S. in Japan agreement.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac on Monday signed a far-reaching bilateral agreement in Tokyo that appeared to be the start of a new trade challenge to the United States in Asia.

Stepped up cooperation in space research, including joint satellite development, was the centrepiece of an accord, called "20 Points For The Year 2000", which Chirac signed with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on the second day of a six-day visit.
It also included agreements to hold annual summits, twice-yearly meetings of foreign ministers and other measures to take ties between the two nations to a loftier level.

"We are two great economic powers, the second and the fourth in the world, and yet our exchanges are insufficient -- Japan is represented in only two percent of the French market and France in only 1.7 percent of the Japanese market," Chirac told reporters after the signing.
Hashimoto said: "We were able to start on making our bilateral relationship the most important one for Asia-Europe cooperation."
Chirac told students at Tokyo's University of Keio that Japan had much to gain from close ties with Europe because his region was becoming an economic power reinforced by a single currency,
"That is why France is an essential partner for you."
Though never explicitly mentioning the United States, Chirac made veiled references to what even some Japanese regard as Washington's economic, strategic and cultural dominance of Japan.
On cultural matters dear to the French government, Chirac called on all "representatives of the major languages to unite in defending that which is most precious: their language".
A source close to the president said many Japanese officials in private expressed hope that a single European currency would soon be in place to counterbalance the power of the dollar.
In today's speech at the university, Chirac encouraged Japan to play a part in the stability of the region.
"Japan has a major role to play in the stability of the region," he said. "Peace in eastern Asia will be the principal challenge for the decades to come," he added.
The source close to the president said that after his talks Chirac believed Japan was now closer to opening markets to certain French products and services,

France is impatient to see Japan Airlines buy European. Though the nine other airlines in Japan have already bought at least one Airbus, JAL -- one of the world's 10 biggest airlines -- has yet to buy even one. JAL uses U.S.-made Boeings.
Under agreements on space research, Japan's space agency NASDA and its French counterpart CNES would work together to develop satellite communications systems.

The accord also envisaged joint ventures between French and Japanese satellite companies, such as the Toshiba-Loral consortium which in 1995 won a French Transport Ministry contract to develop a geostationary weather satellite.
At present, over 70 percent of Japanese satellites are launched by the French-led Arianespace and the agreement aims to consolidate this share.
The two countries' space agencies would also work together on future international space stations and multi-space agency voyages to the moon and to Mars.

This could involve cooperation on Japan's launch in 1998 of a Mars probe, called "Planet B", which would be similar to the ill-fated Russian probe which splashed into the South Pacific on Monday, two days after its launch.

The Russian spacecraft carried almost two dozen instruments that had been intended to probe the red planet's secrets. They had been created by an international consortium including France, Finland, Germany, Hungary and the United States.
